intro: UX researchers typically earn salaries that vary widely based on location, company size, and total compensation packages including equity. Understanding exactly how much do UX researchers make requires moving beyond simple averages to look at specific seniority levels and market sectors.

blocks.text: Why salary benchmarking is difficult for UX researchers

The primary issue is role ambiguity. UX research is often conflated with product design or product management. Because the title lacks a standardized global definition, companies often misprice the role. This leads to massive salary variance across different organizations.

Market volatility also plays a part. The tech sector has seen significant layoffs and a shift in demand since late 2022. This created a disconnect where candidates expect salaries based on the 2021 bubble, while current market offers are often significantly lower.

Misalignment between candidate expectations and actual company budgets.

blocks.text: How to fix your salary benchmarking process

Do not rely on a single source. Combine employer-reported surveys, real-time HRIS data, and self-reported data to build a defensible range. For individuals, platforms like Levels.fyi are best for tech-specific, self-reported compensation data. Glassdoor and Payscale remain useful for broad market averages across various industries.
Better research workflows on your Mac

When you are gathering data, keep your research organized. Use Notion to track the companies you are benchmarking. You can create a database of roles, salary ranges, and equity offers. If you are a manager, ensure you are using tools like Pave or Ravio that integrate with your HRIS to get real-time, industry-specific data.

faq.question: How much do UX researchers make on average?
faq.answer: There is no single average because of role ambiguity and market volatility. You must look at data specific to your location, seniority, and industry sector.

faq.question: Should I include equity in my salary calculations?
faq.answer: Yes. Equity is often the primary driver of the gap between mid-market and top-tier compensation packages.
